name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
title: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
answer: Testing a study design before data collection means checking that a planned analysis can actually answer the question it claims to answer, using simulated or pilot data rather than the real dataset. It covers the choice of outcome, the sample size, the comparison groups, and the handling of missing values, all settled in advance. The aim is to catch design faults while they are still cheap to fix, rather than after months of collection.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Testing a study design before data collection means checking that a planned analysis can actually answer the question it claims to answer, using simulated or pilot data rather than the real dataset. It covers the choice of outcome, the sample size, the comparison groups, and the handling of missing values, all settled in advance. The aim is to catch design faults while they are still cheap to fix, rather than after months of collection.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on ordinary analysis environments: R, Python, or Stata, plus a version control system such as Git to track every change to the plan. Simulation code, random seeds, and package versions are recorded so a colleague can rerun the whole exercise. Where the study will use a shared or restricted dataset, the same pipeline is rehearsed on a synthetic stand-in with the same structure.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical cycle writes the analysis script first, generates data under known assumptions, and runs the script against it to see whether the estimates recover the truth. Sensitivity checks vary the assumptions one at a time, for example the rate of dropout or the strength of a confounder, and record how the conclusions move. The design is revised until the results are stable, and the final script is frozen before any real data arrives.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The pre-data phase is where provenance is easiest to secure, because nothing has been observed yet and the plan can be registered, dated, and shared without disclosing results. Any later deviation from the registered plan should be logged with a reason, so readers can tell a planned test from a post hoc one. Where pilot data are used, their source, permissions, and limits on reuse belong in the same record.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Practice is moving toward treating the design test as a reusable artefact, published alongside the paper so others can rerun it on their own data. Automated checks for common faults, such as underpowered comparisons or undisclosed flexibility in the analysis, are becoming part of review workflows. The direction is a study whose plan, code, and simulated evidence are all inspectable before a single participant is enrolled.
